prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and for its experimental discovery in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep topological insulators as my first choice because it is the discovery on the list that best fits what I think the prize is for: an idea about band topology (the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state) that nature then confirmed. The HgTe quantum wells showed quantised edge conduction, and over roughly two decades many laboratories and probes, transport and ARPES, have agreed with first-principles electronic-structure theory. The concept has changed how materials are classified and has spread to photonics, cold atoms, mechanics and superconductors. It follows the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions without duplicating it, since that prize concerned topological order in model systems and this is a new class of real materials. I have changed one thing from round 1: I now propose Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, with a citation tied to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall state. The chair asked whether such a citation avoids the 3D attribution problem, and I think it does. Kane and Mele wrote the founding Z2 papers together, so dropping Mele splits one theoretical achievement. Hasan's 3D ARPES work is important and I do not belittle it, but it builds on the Fu-Kane-Mele three-dimensional theory, which no trio of ours can credit either. Adding Hasan therefore does not repair the credit chain, it only moves the visible gap. A prize that is coherent about one discovery is better than one that tries to span 2D and 3D and credits neither completely.
statement.case_against: The credit problem has not gone away. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that guided Molenkamp's experiment, and their priority against Kane and Mele has not been checked in this process. Fu and Kane for 3D, and Hasan for the first 3D ARPES observation, are outside the trio, so any three names will look incomplete to part of the community. A prize centred on 2D also leaves out the step that made topological insulators a family of real bulk materials, which I earlier counted as the larger loss, and I still feel that loss. Practical impact is modest compared with conceptual impact. Finally, a prize whose attribution looks arbitrary could damage an otherwise easy scientific case, and the committee should accept that risk knowingly, comparing it with the cleaner two-name credit of B041.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that Kane and Mele's Z2 invariant and quantum spin Hall state are a joint result, that dropping Mele to make room for Hasan splits one achievement, and that a 3D citation would need Fu and Kane and so a different attribution argument.
responses.response: You have persuaded me on this. In round 1 I put the 3D surface states ahead of Mele, because they turned topological insulators into a family of real materials. But the 3D theory is Fu-Kane-Mele, and a trio that credits Hasan without Fu leaves the 3D story as incomplete as before, while it costs us half of the founding theory. I move to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and I would ask that the citation say what Molenkamp is credited for, the experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe wells. I would still note that Hasan's and others' ARPES work is what convinced me nature really has these states in bulk crystals, so I want the minutes to record that this omission is a deliberate choice under a three-person limit and not a judgement on that work.

responses.point: Mehlig says Hasan's 3D ARPES result builds on Fu-Kane-Mele, so adding Hasan only changes which gap is visible, and that the trio of theory pair plus first experimental realisation is the most defensible; he also treats B046's open mechanism as a reason to wait.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning on the trio and have changed my configuration to it. Your point that adding Hasan merely shifts the gap is the sharper form of an argument I had not put together myself. On B046 we agree: I earlier valued it as a theory-predicted flat band that experiment found, but without a settled pairing mechanism a prize now would reward an observation and not an understood phenomenon. I also note you rank only four of the shortlist candidates; the committee should be aware that B032 support is deep but narrow, as you say, and I will not claim the count settles anything.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, asks whether my ranking of B041 seventh is a scientific objection or an overlap objection, and says B041 is the safer prize while the B032 trio is unsettled.
responses.response: My answer is mostly neither, and mostly a different objection: what has the clock taught us about nature? I now accept the overlap argument made by you, Lindroth and Olsson. The comb prize was for the ruler and the 2012 prize for single-particle control, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice, with many neutral atoms interrogated at once and the trap shift engineered to cancel, is a distinct idea. What remains is that millimetre-scale redshift measurements, and bounds on varying constants and dark matter, so far confirm known physics. That is a legitimate result, but not yet a discovery about nature in the sense I mean. It is a scientific reservation, and a modest one, so I will treat B041 as a respectable fallback, my first alternative. On safety: I take the point that B041's credit is cleaner, but I think the one-name question in B032 is now answered by the argument above, so I do not accept that it is safer on the science.

responses.point: Lindroth says the magic-wavelength condition is a quantitative atomic-structure prediction that was then verified, that 1e-18 agreement across laboratories is a stronger test than most, and that the committee should say what is learned about nature in the citation.
responses.response: That is a fair correction to my round-1 framing. I mean that a prediction later confirmed by experiment is what I value, and the magic-wavelength condition qualifies, as does the cross-laboratory 1e-18 agreement. I also accept that many-body effects in the lattice are controlled and understood, and that this is real physics. My residual hesitation is that the headline tests, gravitational redshift over millimetres and constraints on constants, have so far found no deviation. If the committee wished to prefer B041, I would support a citation worded around the lattice clock only, not clocks in general, so it does not read as a third clock prize, and I would not obstruct it.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock, with Katori on concept and first demonstration and Ye on bringing the platform to record performance, is the clearest case of a new measurement capability, that its results are reproduced independently, and that the Katori-Ye credit is clean.
responses.response: I agree on the evidence and on the structure of the credit; the independent agreement of Sr, Yb and Hg clocks is the best maturity argument in the whole shortlist. Where we still differ is on what weighs more when the two candidates point in different directions. For me a new state of matter that was predicted and found outweighs a measurement capability whose discoveries about nature are still prospective. I would not call that a criterion every member must share, and I see a split between B041 and B032 that rests on a real difference in taste. The pending redefinition of the second does not worry me as a maturity condition. The physics and the inter-laboratory agreement are already in hand.

uncertainties: The priority chronology of Kane-Mele against Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang for the HgTe proposal, which I have not verified, and whether it should change the credited theory names.
Whether the committee accepts that Hasan and other ARPES groups, and Fu, are left out of the 3D story by a deliberate choice under the three-person limit.
Whether members who put B041 first will accept B032 on the strength of the discovery-in-nature argument if the attribution question is settled as Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and the other way round.
Dates for the first strontium lattice clock and the first 1e-18 evaluations, quoted by others from memory and not checked, which matter if the committee falls back on B041.
Whether the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene will be clarified in time to change my view of B046.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My Princeton PhD supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are not credited in any shortlisted entry, and my research in string theory and cosmology is far from the condensed-matter, atomic and astroparticle candidates. As Secretary I have commissioned no expert report for this simulated process, and I have no known tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, Katori or Ye. This is unchanged from round 1.
